title: State of jazz and survival of New York clubs
summary: She cannot judge whether jazz has grown or shrunk, but clubs struggle with rents and some mix genres or rely on a diner like Iridium.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: I sometimes ask the question what is the state of jazz in your opinion?

Yeah, that comes up a lot. It’s really hard for me to say. I think jazz — I mean it’s never going to have the place of other genres that get millions of people interested. That’s just what it is. I don’t know whether it’s gotten better or worse or more popular or less © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

popular, I just don’t feel like I can judge that. I know it’s very hard for jazz clubs to stay alive financially. The rents in New York are off the wall. You know, they open, they close, if they want to stay alive they have to pretty much do something else like the Iridium is downstairs from a very successful diner where they have singing waiters, and they’re both owned by the same person so that’s how they get most of their income.
Oh, so one helps pay for the other.

The Stardust Diner or something, yeah. And then some of them start to mix genres and then they don’t — they get sort of less interested in jazz. And that’s annoying to us, and that’s a trend, and I guess there’s not much we can do about it.
